To make caramelized onions real fast: TIP. I did them perfectly last day so want to share, fast, ez, don't even need to constantly stir BUT I imagine that's up to ur pan, if it sticks then u would have to.

Basically, for 1 cup of diced onions, put half a cup of water in your pan, half the salt u'll use in the recipe, and if u were to use smth that would benefit from being boiled (like bay leaves) that too. Only that.

Put all the onions, stir well, cover with a transparent lid preferably, and leave it there at high heat until it starts to boil (to speed up the boiling).

then uncover them and let all the liquid reduce, once there is no more liquid left, add the oil and stir them,  then cover with a lid and leave them there until they start sizzling, then take the lid off and stir them here and there to make sure they don't stick.

Been working in the produce distribution industry for 5 years. There are 2 reasons for this.

#1 - Costco has a contract with a national distributor to buy romaine on contract. What that means is the national distributor gives Costco a price that is good for 1+ year. Doesn’t matter the season. So if the market price goes way up Costco pays less, if the market prices goes down, Costco pays more. Distributors sometimes lose money on these contract deals but not usually. It averages out over the year.

#2 - Groceries stores often use what is called a loss leader, meaning a product that will actually lose them money when sold but will lead customers to the store.

I would be willing to bet it is mainly reason #1. Market price on romaine right now is awful, it will come down in the coming weeks. If it is worth it to you to save $26 going to Costco for that one item by all means do it!

To keep cucumbers fresh for longer (at least what I do) I give them a good wash with tap water, then soak in cold water for 30 minutes (this allows the cucumbers to absorb some water that evaporated and makes them firmer and more crunchy). My cucumbers last for about 2 weeks this way.

Get a dehydrator if you don't already have one. Walmart has them fairly cheap, Cabellas has more high end ones. Make sure the produce is completely dry before you package it after dehydrating. A little moisture will cause things to mold. So, over dry, then pack up and use as you wish. My dehydrated veggies last a long time, I have some that are fine 5 years in. Just don't expose them to much light, including pantry and sunlight, once dried. Keep in a dark location. Carrots dehydrate nicely, shred them, blanche them and dry. Strawberries also and they freeze nicely. I've done lemons, too. No experience with grapes or cukes. But dried grapes are raisins, so have at it!
